abstract: Climate risks prompt the public to prefer environmental protection and detest environmental pollution. We examine the impact of such attitudes on corporate environmental decision-making. The findings indicate that public preference for environmental protection can induce corporate greenwashing, while public aversion to environmental pollution can inhibit corporate greenwashing. More importantly, compared to public preference for green, public aversion to brown plays a more important role in corporate greenwashing decisions, suggesting that firms follow the loss aversion principle when making environmentally unethical decisions. Mechanism analyses reveal that public preference for environmental protection can induce corporate greenwashing by stimulating firms' motivation to cater to the public, while public aversion to environmental pollution can inhibit corporate greenwashing by triggering environmental opinion pressure. Further analyses indicate that the inhibitory effect of public aversion to brown is more pronounced in strictly environmentally regulated firms, while the promoting effect of public preference for green is attenuated in high-transparency firms. These findings reveal the heterogeneous impacts of public environmental attitudes on corporate environmental decision-making.
title: Like green and dislike brown: How do public environmental attitudes impact corporate greenwashing?

abstract: Gender disparities in household electricity consumption and appliance ownership have important implications for social equity and energy planning. This paper uses an instrumental-variable approach to study how income and financial access shape these disparities using nationally representative household surveys from India, Kazakhstan, and the Kyrgyz Republic. By comparing countries with different income levels and financial-access conditions, the analysis highlights both common mechanisms and country-specific patterns in gender disparities in energy outcomes. In India, among low-income households, female-headed households have a higher electricity expenditure share than male-headed households. In Kazakhstan, no significant average gender gap in electricity expenditure is observed, although a modest gap emerges among the highest-income households, where female-headed households have a lower electricity expenditure share. In the Kyrgyz Republic, female-headed households consistently have a lower expenditure share than male-headed households, and the gap widens at higher income levels. The relationship between financial access and appliance ownership varies across countries and appliances. Among households that did not own the selected appliances when first surveyed, financial access is positively associated with acquiring all three appliances examined in India and the Kyrgyz Republic during the survey period. Gender differences in this relationship are concentrated in washing-machine acquisition: the female–male difference is statistically significant in the Kyrgyz Republic and marginally significant in India. Gender differences for the other appliances are not statistically significant. The findings are consistent with gender differences in liquidity constraints when households consider appliance purchases, although the underlying household decision-making mechanisms are not directly observed. Expanding financial access may reshape the gender distribution of future appliance ownership and residential electricity demand. These patterns highlight the importance of monitoring electricity expenditure burdens and financial access by household-head gender, while recognizing that the effectiveness of specific policy interventions requires separate evaluation.
title: Income and gender disparities in electricity expenditure and appliance ownership: Evidence from three household surveys in South and Central Asia

abstract: In the last decade, there has been a surge of text-mining applications in the information systems literature. In these applications, researchers typically construct independent variables from documents by various text-mining techniques. The most prominent example could be using online review sentiments to investigate online word-of-mouth issues. Typically, most documents contain information richer than the independent variable, and researchers may construct control variables from the same documents to alleviate endogeneity issues. However, researchers need to manually craft these variables, and this process may not guarantee that all the important confounding factors are extracted and included in the regression model with a correct functional form. If useful textual information is overlooked and a valid identification strategy is not available, the omitted variable bias may occur. To solve this challenge, we propose a novel model that utilizes text embedding based on the state-of-the-art neural network language model (i.e., bidirectional encoder representations from transformers (BERT)) to automatically create a new control variable vector for controlling latent confounding factors in the absence of a valid identification strategy. Moreover, our approach can be considered a semiparametric approach in that our model contains a linear term of the key independent variable and an unknown functional term of the textual control variables. Our approach extends the semiparametric framework, double machine learning, by introducing a novel Neyman-orthogonal loss function in an integrated deep neural network to minimize the estimation bias. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of controlling textual control variables by text embedding and improving the estimation performance by the novel loss function. This paper was accepted by Anindya Ghose, information systems. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.04758 .
publisher: Institute for Operations Research and the Management Sciences (INFORMS)
title: Correcting the Unobserved Textual Confounding Factors in Regression by BERT and Partially Linear Regression

abstract: Trade credit is traditionally viewed as increasing supplier risk, because delayed payments expose suppliers to buyer uncertainties. Using a stylized game-theoretic model, we show that this conventional wisdom can be overturned when a supplier is dual channel: operating a direct channel that sells to end customers in addition to an indirect channel that sells to an industry peer who serves the same market. Compared with zero trade credit provision where the supplier requires cash on delivery (COD), we observe empirically that high trade credit provision can lead to lower risk for the dual-channel supplier. We propose a possible mechanism for this risk mitigation effect—pooling: When the market overlap between the supplier and its peer buyer is sufficiently high, the random split of the overlapping market creates negative association between the supplier’s direct channel sales and the buyer’s trade credit payment. Trade credit does not always mitigate risk for dual-channel suppliers. If the supplier’s debt level is high, our theory predicts that trade credit exacerbates risk. We find empirical evidence consistent with our theoretical predictions using data on U.S. manufacturing firms that sell to their industry peers. The positive association between trade credit provision and bankruptcy risk is dampened or even reversed once a supplier begins selling to peer firms. This risk mitigation effect is stronger among suppliers with lower leverage and greater market overlap with their buyers. For highly financially constrained suppliers, trade credit provision is associated with an increase in bankruptcy risk after the supplier becomes dual channel. This paper was accepted by Jayashankar Swaminathan, operations management. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.03142 .
publisher: Institute for Operations Research and the Management Sciences (INFORMS)
title: Reducing Risk Through Trade Credit: Theory and Evidence from Dual-Channel Suppliers

abstract: We study factor models that combine latent factors with firm characteristics and propose a new framework for modeling, estimating, and inferring pricing errors. Following Zhang (2024), our approach decomposes mispricing into two distinct components: inside alpha, explained by firm characteristics but orthogonal to factor exposures, and outside alpha, orthogonal to both factors and characteristics. Our model generalizes those developed recently such as Kelly et al. (2019) and Zhang (2024), resolving issues of orthogonality, basis dependence, and unit sensitivity. Methodologically, we develop estimators grounded in low-rank methods with explicit debiasing, providing closed-form solutions and a rigorous inferential theory that accommodates a growing number of characteristics and relaxes standard assumptions on sample dimensions. Empirically, using U.S. stock returns from 2000 to 2019, we document strong evidence of both inside and outside alphas, with the former showing industry-level comovements and the latter reflecting idiosyncratic shocks beyond firm fundamentals. Our framework thus unifies statistical and characteristic-based approaches to factor modeling, offering both theoretical advances and new insights into the structure of pricing errors. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. Funding: This research was supported by the National Science Foundation [Grant DMS-2052955]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.04971 .
publisher: Institute for Operations Research and the Management Sciences (INFORMS)
title: Inferential Theory for Pricing Errors with Latent Factors and Firm Characteristics

abstract: Mixed-nationality founding teams bring together heterogeneous, hard-to-replicate bundles of human capital and country-specific ties through their cross-national networks, providing a distinctive foundation for building successful ventures. Yet these connections may be vulnerable to nonmarket shocks. This study examines whether geopolitical conflicts and disputes between the countries of origin of immigrant founders affect the formation of new ventures. Leveraging data on the founders of start-ups established in Great Britain and global information on conflicts and disputes, I find that such tensions reduce the likelihood that nationals of hostile countries cofound firms together. The evidence is more consistent with social mechanisms and, particularly, the erosion of interpersonal relationships than with diminished access to cross-country resources or the loss of entrepreneurial opportunities. Start-ups of both low and high quality are affected, including in sectors that depend heavily on skilled human capital, such as high-tech and business services. The negative effect is substantially attenuated for nationality pairs that are heavily colocated across local areas and for founders with prior social exposure to individuals from the opposing nationality, indicating that interpersonal ties can buffer against geopolitical shocks. Conflicts do not affect the exit of existing firms, and the decline in mixed-nationality entrepreneurship is not offset by alternative team configurations such as solo ventures or those formed with conationals, natives, or individuals from third-party countries. This paper was accepted by Alfonso Gambardella, business strategy. Funding: I gratefully acknowledge funding from the Institute for Leadership and Social Impact at Georgia Institute of Technology. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.04559 .
publisher: Institute for Operations Research and the Management Sciences (INFORMS)
title: Echoes of Discord: The Effects of Global Conflicts and Disputes on Entrepreneurship

abstract: Agricultural greenhouse gas mitigation depends on technological progress, farmers’ skills, and their production decisions. Using county-level panel data from 2010 to 2023, we exploit the staggered rollout of China’s professional farmer training demonstration policy as a quasi-natural experiment. The policy reduced county-level agricultural greenhouse gas emissions by approximately 1.4% on average. The reductions were larger outside major grain-producing areas, in non-poor counties, and in counties with greater agricultural competitiveness. The policy was associated with lower fertilizer application and crop residue burning intensities, more agricultural innovation activity, and increases in the number of agricultural machinery businesses and green agricultural cooperatives. These findings point to changes in production practices, agricultural technological innovation, and the development of agricultural businesses as potential mitigation channels. The results inform the design of professional farmer training policies tailored to local conditions.

abstract: Using panel data for 276 Chinese cities from 2005 to 2023, this study employs a double machine learning approach to examine how a dual-pilot energy transition policy affects the synergistic development of economic agglomeration and environmental performance. The results show that the dual-pilot policy significantly enhances such synergistic development and generates stronger effects than either pilot implemented alone, indicating positive policy complementarity. Mechanism analysis identifies artificial intelligence adoption, interregional technology flows, and industrial co-agglomeration as three key channels. The effects are more pronounced in regions characterized by stricter environmental regulation, stronger financial institutional constraints, and higher levels of market development. Spatial analysis reveals a negative spatial association, suggesting interregional competition induced by the policy. Further analysis identifies a carbon rebound effect: improvements in the synergistic development of economic agglomeration and environmental performance are accompanied by a partial erosion of potential carbon-reduction gains, particularly in central China. These findings provide empirical evidence for optimizing energy transition policy design, strengthening supporting institutional arrangements, and promoting cross-regional cooperation.

abstract: Compulsory asset conversion changes household resources through asset loss, compensation payments and replacement needs. This paper examines household adjustment following housing demolition and land expropriation in China. Cohort-interacted event studies use the China Family Panel Studies from 2010 to 2022, complemented by a separate demolition analysis using linked China Household Finance Survey data. Demolition is followed by a reporting-wave increase of approximately CNY 13,500 in consumption excluding housing on a common sample. A later-wave comparison also shows a positive inverse-hyperbolic-sine response after excluding measured housing and durable-related outlays. Recorded income gains concentrate in transfers without comparable wage gains. For land expropriation, the pooled post-event net-wealth difference between the highest and lowest first-reported nominal compensation groups is approximately CNY 218,000. Demolition also combines asset conversion with relocation. By separating expenditure composition, income recording and balance-sheet distribution, the analysis clarifies household adjustment to compulsory asset conversion. The findings support evaluating compensation through the resources and asset services households rebuild, alongside the payment received.

abstract: Fuel prices are visible components of household expenditure, making them an informative setting for studying long-horizon price expectations. This paper asks how accurately households project the price of their own vehicle’s fuel and how those projections relate to their broader price beliefs. A 2015 survey of 2,000 Korean new-car buyers elicited fuel-price and general-price expectations at one-, five-, and ten-year horizons. Their fuel-price forecasts are evaluated against realized gasoline, diesel, and LPG prices through 2025. The main comparison uses current-price persistence, a rule that carries each respondent’s reported current nominal fuel price forward without change. Across these completed horizons, respondent mean absolute errors are 2.27 to 2.98 times those of the benchmark. Fuel-price and general-price expectations are also strongly associated in direction. Together, these findings describe the numerical performance of expectations for a familiar expenditure item alongside the broader price outlook accompanying them. The study adds long-horizon validation evidence to research on salient prices and household inflation expectations. For this Korean cohort and price realization, it also informs how reported expectations are interpreted and used in projections of future operating costs.
title: Long-horizon household fuel-price expectations: general-price beliefs and ex post evidence from Korea

abstract: This paper examines how vehicle tax systems designed to reduce emissions affect automobile market outcomes in Indonesia. Using detailed vehicle sales data, I estimate an equilibrium model and simulate market outcomes under the two tax regimes. The results suggest that reverting to the old tax regime increases the sales-weighted CO2 emissions per kilometer of new vehicle sales by 1.79%, primarily through reduced sales of vehicles in the lowest quartile of emission rates.
title: Vehicle taxation and emissions reduction: Evidence from Indonesia

abstract: Negative electricity prices create market-relevant risks for trading, bidding, renewable revenues, and flexibility valuation. Quantile regression-based postprocessing is a widely used approach for converting point forecasts into predictive distributions. We show that the standard specification, which imposes a single linear relationship between the point forecast and predictive quantiles, can become structurally incoherent when the conditioning point forecast is negative. In such cases, the resulting predictive distribution may exhibit not only ordinary quantile crossing, where adjacent quantiles are in the wrong order, but also a severe version of crossing, which we refer to as t a i l - q u a n t i l e i n v e r s i o n . This can reverse downside and upside risk signals. To address this problem, we propose sign-dependent QR-based postprocessing specifications that allow the quantile function to differ between positive and negative point forecasts. Using German day-ahead electricity prices as the main empirical setting, we show that these specifications improve predictive accuracy, particularly for negative point forecasts and extreme probability levels. When combined with joint estimation across quantiles, they eliminate quantile crossing and tail-quantile inversion. A robustness analysis for the U.S. SPP market confirms the main coherence results, although the gains in predictive accuracy are less pronounced. We demonstrate the economic relevance of the forecasts using a battery arbitrage strategy, where probabilistic forecasts improve trading performance relative to a point-forecast benchmark and the sign-dependent specifications can provide additional gains. The results demonstrate that the sign of the point forecast should be explicitly accounted for when constructing probabilistic forecasts in markets where negative prices can occur.
title: Quantile regression postprocessing with negative electricity price forecasts

abstract: For a global sample, the study examines the impact that the Covid-motivated 2020 lockdowns had on terrorist attacks. We are particularly interested in how lockdowns differentially affected domestic versus transnational terrorism because some Covid-based restrictions are likely more suited to one form of terrorism. Identification exploits cross-country variation in the timing and stringency of lockdown policies, while controlling for country-specific time-varying factors and common monthly shocks through high-dimensional fixed effects. We find that stricter lockdowns significantly reduce total and domestic terrorism, whereas transnational terrorist attacks remain largely unaffected. Preliminary evidence suggests that the decline in domestic terrorism is temporary, with attacks rebounding once lockdowns end. Disaggregating the stringency index further shows that most individual containment measures reduce total and domestic terrorism, consistent with lockdown restrictions exerting a deterrence as vulnerabilities are protected. These findings provide new evidence on how large-scale mobility restrictions influence terrorists’ behavior and highlight important differences between domestic and transnational terrorism.
title: Covid-19, lockdown stringency, and terrorist attacks

abstract: Harberger (1971) established three postulates that provided the professional standards for applied welfare economics. While empirical economics has advanced significantly in the fifty-five years since, the profession has yet to establish a corresponding set of standards for the policy assessments and recommendations that stem from this research. This paper proposes three new postulates for applied welfare economics: (1) explicit articulation of the underlying policy issue to avoid impulsive or passive analysis; (2) an empirical assessment that integrates both prospective and retrospective counterfactual evidence; and (3) a search for welfare-maximizing or least-cost solutions that explicitly account for potential government failure and market self-correction. These postulates are operationalized through a protocol—a strategic decision tree designed to bridge the gap between causal identification and professional policy recommendations. I argue that the adoption of these postulates would improve the reliability of economists’ policy recommendations and credibility among policymakers.
title: Beyond Harberger: three postulates for economic policy assessments and recommendations

abstract: We use a large-scale survey from Denmark to construct firm-level measures of the working environment that capture its physical, psychological, and social dimensions. First, to validate these measures, we show that firms with better working environments perform better in unannounced workplace inspections conducted by a government agency. Second, using register data, we show that firms with better working environments have longer employee tenure, and that their employees are less likely to be hospitalized or experience work-related accidents. Finally, firms with better working environments have higher labor productivity and, ultimately, greater profitability. Collectively, our findings suggest that improving firms’ working environments can benefit both employees and shareholders.
title: The economics of working environments: evidence from linked survey and register data‡

abstract: A buyer seeks to procure a good or service from one of two ex ante identical suppliers who privately know their costs and whether they possess evidence verifying those costs. We characterize profit-maximizing procurement mechanisms with and without admissible cost evidence. Allowing evidence weakly raises buyer profit but can reduce total surplus, even when procurement becomes more frequent. The optimal mechanism favors evidence holders and may select a more costly supplier. Allowing cost evidence improves welfare for sufficiently small procurement benefits and lowers it for sufficiently large benefits.
title: Cost evidence and welfare in optimal procurement

abstract: This article examines the welfare consequences of industrial policies aimed at boosting domestic manufacturing in developing countries, focusing on the Indian government's tariff policy for mobile handset production. We develop a structural model of India's mobile handset industry, where firms endogenously decide supply chain alternatives, product sets, and prices. Our counterfactual simulations indicate that the status quo import tariff on ready‐to‐use handsets significantly increases local assembly operations. However, a lower tariff of around 8% would maintain similar assembly levels and significantly enhance consumer surplus. An additional input import tariff on handset components discourages firms from relocating operations to India, potentially undermining the policy's goal.
title: Domestic Tariffs and Consumer Welfare in Developing Countries: Evidence From India

abstract: This paper uses global, harmonized micro data from labor force surveys to document the labor market effects of economic crises. There is a close correspondence between severe labor market downturns and a small set of crisis events, notably banking panics, sudden stops, and house price busts. Crises fall disproportionately on marginal workers – younger, less-educated, and lower-earnings workers – and employment losses are concentrated in the manufacturing and construction sectors. We provide aggregate and distributional evidence on several mechanisms discussed in the literature, including exchange rate regimes and devaluation.
title: Labor market anatomy of a macroeconomic crisis

abstract: Forest ecological compensation schemes play a critical role in incentivizing forest conservation and restoration, yet they remain heavily dependent on government fiscal transfers. Such reliance raises concerns regarding long-term financial sustainability, incentive stability, and the limited participation of private capital in forest governance. In response to these challenges, this paper proposes a structured financing mechanism that integrates forest carbon sinks into a hybrid public-market structure designed to complement existing compensation policies. The proposed mechanism conceptualizes forest carbon sequestration as a revenue source within a structured financing architecture. The simulation examines project cash flow, investor returns, and risk exposure under specified carbon-price and ecological scenarios. The results suggest potential financial feasibility under the modeled assumptions and indicate that the proposed risk-sharing structure may improve the conditions for private capital participation. The framework therefore offers a potential pathway for complementing fiscal support with market-based financing for forest ecological compensation. The findings provide policy-relevant insights into the design of more resilient and scalable financing mechanisms to support forest conservation and carbon sequestration objectives.
title: Mobilizing private capital for forest ecological compensation: A carbon sink-based hybrid financing mechanism

abstract: Distributional conflicts over benefits are widespread in land institutional reforms, yet how they affect institutional change and what role the state plays remain insufficiently explained. This study integrates distributional conflict (equity) and social production (efficiency) into one framework, develops a sequential evolutionary game among the central government, local governments, and farmers, and examines the interactions among state goals, distributional conflict, and institutional change through China’s reform experience. The results show that: (1) Distributional contradictions can coexist with institutional stability. When the existing institution has a strong efficiency advantage consistent with the state’s core goals and distributional contradictions have not been fully translated into conflict behavior, the system tends toward a strategy state in which the existing institution is maintained. (2) When distributional contradictions develop into conflict behavior, the state places greater weight on equity while efficiency remains dominant, and the existing institution retains its efficiency advantage, distributional conflict can create conditions for gradual reform strategies. Historical reforms exhibit gradual adjustment through pilot programs and partial institutional changes. (3) Formal institutional change does not depend on conflict intensity alone. It depends on the parties’ relative conflict capacity, the equity improvements and efficiency losses generated by conflict, and the state’s goal trade-offs. When the utility gains from improved equity are sufficient to offset the efficiency utility losses, the institutional change strategy may gain an advantage. The historical evolution of China’s rural land transfer rights reform for non-agricultural use is consistent with these mechanisms. Accordingly, this study recommends strengthening social surveys of land benefit distribution conflicts and comprehensive assessments of the equity and efficiency effects of land institutions.

abstract: I develop a theory of state-dependent signal extraction in price setting. Firms infer how much sectoral price movements reflect persistent aggregate or transitory sector-specific disturbances. When inflation is low relative to sectoral variation, sticky-price firms discount competitor movements because following transitory movements risks leaving them mispriced. As inflation rises relative to sectoral noise, firms increasingly attribute these movements to aggregate shocks and sticky firms respond more strongly. UK micro-price data support these predictions: below approximately 1.9% sectoral inflation, sticky firms respond less to competitors than flexible firms; above it, the gap closes. This convergence generates state-dependent aggregate inflation dynamics.
title: A Signal-Extraction Theory of Inflation Pass-Through

abstract: We analyze firms’ perceptions of their cost of capital using hand-collected data. The perceived cost of capital is associated with the allocation of capital across firms. In a model with inefficient financial markets, firms can maximize their current market value by setting their perceived cost of capital equal to the expected returns on their debt and equity. In the data, little variation in firms’ perceived cost of capital can be justified by variation in expected returns, suggesting that firms do not follow this market-value maximization benchmark. Alternatively, firms may aim to maximize their “fair value” corrected for financial market inefficiencies. In the data, a fair-value benchmark (based on the CAPM) can justify half the variation in the perceived cost of capital. However, most of the variation can be justified by the beliefs of financial analysts about expected returns. Using a quantitative model, we find that the observed distortions in the perceived cost of capital can substantially impact capital allocation and thereby reduce aggregate productivity.
title: Firms’ Perceived Cost of Capital

abstract: Many countries use a reverse charge mechanism (RC) in the value added tax (VAT) system to combat tax evasion in specific high-risk sectors. The RC shifts the liability to remit VAT from the seller to the buyer. We study the adoption of RC in the construction sector in Finland in 2011 using tax return data on the universe of Finnish firms. Using a difference-in-differences design, we find that reported net VAT liabilities in the construction sector increased by 5%. Furthermore, we find that the adoption of RC increases reported payroll taxes and income tax withholding, suggesting spillovers from VAT enforcement to other tax bases. Changing the remittance policy decreased VAT evasion among small subcontractors that provide services for large firms. Taken together, our results and conceptual framework show that shifting remittance liability can reduce tax evasion even in a VAT system in which the paper trail mechanism already deters it, provided that downstream firms are relatively compliant.
title: Improving VAT compliance by switching who remits the tax: Evidence from construction firms

abstract: This paper examines the consequences of site aggregation in multi-site travel cost models, focusing on the aggregation of the non-focal alternatives into a broad “other recreation” option. We first develop a theoretical framework identifying the conditions under which aggregation may bias parameter and welfare estimates. We then use a simple Monte Carlo simulation to show that bias depends on (a) individual-level preference heterogeneity, (b) correlation between the utility of the aggregated alternatives and that of the focal ones, and (c) the choice share of the aggregated alternatives. We also investigate the impact of aggregation empirically, by estimating a model of coastal recreation using data from more than 9,000 choice occasions across 176 recreation sites in Maui, Hawaiʻi. We compare estimates obtained using all sites and after aggregating all non-coastal sites, using two estimation strategies: the repeated conditional logit model (CLM) and the two-stage approach. We find that aggregating non-coastal sites has negligible effects on both parameter estimates and welfare measures. The two-stage approach produces welfare estimates similar to those of the CLM for site-closure scenarios, but is substantially less precise for scenarios involving changes in site quality. Estimated resident welfare losses arising from sediment runoff causing coastal brown water events range from approximately $6 million to $11 million per year, depending on the scenario and the modelling assumptions.
title: Site Aggregation in Recreational Demand Modeling with an Application to the Impact of Sediments Runoffs in Coastal Waters

abstract: Can tourism-oriented place-based policies stimulate corporate green innovation? Using 21,921 firm-year observations of Chinese A-share listed firms across 240 prefecture-level cities from 2003 to 2024, this study exploits the staggered designation of China’s 5 A National Tourist Attractions as a quasi-natural experiment. Staggered difference-in-differences estimates show that 5 A designation significantly increases corporate green patenting. Further analyses reveal three complementary pathways: designation heightens local government environmental attention, strengthens public environmental attention, and enhances firms’ environmental orientation, all of which are positively associated with corporate green innovation. Subsample analyses reveal variation in the estimated innovation response across firms with different tourism relevance, absorptive capacity, and pollution characteristics. Spatial analyses further indicate that the innovation response extends beyond designated cities through cross-city linkages. These findings demonstrate that tourism quality certification can reshape firms’ environmental innovation incentives beyond its primary tourism objective, broadening the policy foundations of green technological change and highlighting the environmental innovation consequences of place-based development policies.

title: Tourism designation and green innovation: Evidence from China’s 5A National Tourist Attractions

abstract: Although electric vehicles (EVs) are a climate-friendly alternative to internal combustion engine vehicles (ICEVs), EV adoption is challenged by higher up-front procurement prices. Existing discourse attributes this price differential to high battery costs and assumes that lowering these costs to below $100/kWh will create upfront cost parity between EVs and ICEVs. Does existing data support such reasoning? What factors beyond battery cost impact EV prices? And what relative influence do battery and non-battery factors have on price? Leveraging data for over 400 EV models and trims sold in the United States (US) between 2011 and 2023, we address these questions. We find that, counterintuitively, the average manufacturer's suggested retail price (MSRP) of EVs has increased over time despite declining EV battery costs. During the same period, we observe substantial increases in horsepower and the number of vehicle features, both of which are significant predictors of rising EV prices. Moreover, our analyses suggest that future reductions in pack-level battery costs are unlikely to deliver price parity between EVs and ICEVs. We estimate that were battery packs to cost $100/kWh, a threshold considered pivotal to achieving ICEV-EV price parity and motivating widespread EV affordability, average EV prices would decline by just $5088. These findings warrant attention as decarbonization efforts increasingly emphasize EVs as a pathway for complying with domestic and international climate agreements.
title: Enumerating predictors of electric vehicle prices

abstract: This study examines how strengthening creditor rights can have unintended capital-market consequences by reshaping investors' perceptions of firms whose controlling shareholders (promoters) pledge shares. Exploiting India's Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), enacted in 2016, as a quasi-natural experiment, we find no significant pre-reform association between pledging and crash risk, consistent with the signaling benefits and agency costs of pledging offsetting each other. Following IBC implementation, however, pledging firms experienced significantly higher crash risk, consistent with heightened creditor enforcement increasing the risk of promoter control loss. This increase is more pronounced in regions with higher district judicial capacity, providing further evidence consistent with the enforcement mechanism. Channel analysis supports the ownership-loss mechanism, although the evidence from ownership-based subsample tests is mixed. Turnover interactions further suggest that investor disagreement amplifies the post-IBC increase in crash risk among pledging firms experiencing deteriorating promoter ownership. The increase is also more pronounced among firms with excessive pledging but weaker among dividend-paying firms. Overall, our findings show that stronger creditor rights make promoter control fragility more consequential, increasing investor disagreement and crash risk, highlighting the unintended capital-market consequences of reforms designed to strengthen creditor protection.
title: Strengthening pledgee rights and stock price crash risk

abstract: Long viewed as a flexible and tax-efficient way to return cash to shareholders, share repurchases have recently come under growing public criticism, triggering political and regulatory responses. We find that public sentiment, as reflected in negative media coverage of share repurchases, deters share repurchase activity. Political risk is an important channel for this relation, as politically sensitive firms exhibit a greater reduction in repurchase activity in response to negative public sentiment. When we analyze the consequences of sentiment-induced share repurchase reductions, we find that the reduced repurchases exacerbate, rather than mitigate, agency problems. Instead of switching to dividends, firms reduce overall payout, hold excess cash at a discounted market valuation, and pursue inefficient investments, all of which suggests diminished shareholder welfare. Taken together, our evidence shows that in a political economy skeptical of corporations, public sentiment can influence corporate payout policies, even at the expense of shareholder interests.
title: Public Sentiment and Share Repurchases

abstract: As global green development advances, growing environmental concerns and the challenge of long-term sustainability are threatening supply chain resilience. The growing green preferences embedded in inter-firm collaboration make observable and trustworthy green transformation a key driver reshaping supply chain relationships. Drawing on Green Factory Certification (GFC) as a quasi-natural experiment, this study examines how verifiable green transformation shapes supply chain resilience within customer and supplier networks. The results indicate that obtaining GFC significantly strengthens firms’ supply chain resilience. The primary channels include improving ESG performance, enhancing operational efficiency, and promoting supply chain diversification and geographic dispersion. Heterogeneity analyses reveal that the marginal effect is stronger for firms with weaker green innovation, digital capabilities, and internal control systems. Overall, this study provides robust empirical evidence that government green certification contributes to supply chains resilience. It deepens understanding of the interplay between green transformation and supply chain resilience from the perspectives of both financial and non-financial performance, as well as supply chain resource allocation.

abstract: The study examines the multiscale, nonlinear relationship between ESG-related uncertainty (ESGUI) and Chinese sectoral equity markets. To this end, it employs a novel multi-frequency quantile correlation approach (MFQC), which decomposes the correlation across market conditions and timescales. Based on data from August 2011 to January 2025, the empirical outcomes show asymmetric correlations between bull and bear markets, and across short- and long-term investment horizons. The results underscore that sectors differ in the sign of their association with ESGUI, and dependence is concentrated at longer horizons. A wavelet nonparametric quantile causality approach corroborates this horizon structure, with significance attenuating towards the distributional tails in several sectors. These patterns indicate that ESG-related uncertainty is reflected in sectoral valuations at low rather than high frequencies, with implications for regulatory design and portfolio allocation.

abstract: This study examines whether corporate digital transformation alters firms’ reliance on labour outsourcing. Using 41,843 firm-year observations for Chinese non-financial A-share listed firms from 2012 to 2025, we examine both the probability of reporting labour outsourcing expenditures and the ratio of outsourcing expenditures to employee compensation. We find that greater digital transformation is associated with a significantly lower probability of reporting labour outsourcing expenditures and a lower outsourcing expenditure ratio. The findings are robust to propensity-score matching, alternative measures of digital transformation, tests addressing strategic disclosure, and longer-lag specifications. We also examine endogeneity using a historical-telecommunications instrumental variable. Mechanism analyses indicate that digital transformation is associated with greater asset specificity and lower supply–demand volatility, consistent with transaction-cost and operational-flexibility mechanisms. The negative relationship is stronger among non-state-owned firms, labour-intensive firms, less financially constrained firms, firms facing greater product-market competition, and firms located in regions with lower levels of marketization. Overall, the evidence suggests that digital transformation reduces firms’ reliance on external labour sourcing, revealing a labour-related dimension of firm boundary adjustment.

abstract: This paper investigates trading mechanisms for efficiently (re)allocating a good to agents who face liquidity constraints and have private information about their valuation. I derive a necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of ex post efficient, interim incentive compatible, interim individually rational, ex post budget balanced and ex post liquidity constrained trading mechanisms. Applying the framework to partnership dissolution problems, I show that efficient buyouts are more likely when initial ownership shares are tilted toward less liquid partners and away from more financially flexible ones. For practical implementation, I propose an auction format that implements the liquidity-constrained mechanism in a simple and operational way. Finally, I demonstrate that increasing the number of participants raises the liquidity resources required to sustain efficient trade, suggesting that larger markets may exacerbate financial frictions rather than alleviate them.
title: Asymmetric Information, Liquidity Constraints, and Efficient Trade

abstract: This paper provides identification results for the causal effect of treatment on binary outcomes, considering both ordered (nesting binary treatments as a special case) and continuous treatments. Within a quantile regression framework, treatment endogeneity is characterized by the joint distribution (copula) of unobserved errors. Identification is achieved using instrumental variables and a shape restriction on the copula.
title: Identification of the causal effect of treatment on binary outcomes

abstract: Two formats are commonly used to report grouped income data. The first provides group population shares and income bounds which can be represented as a histogram. The second presents group population shares with income shares (or mean incomes) which can be represented as a (generalised) Lorenz curve. The purpose of this paper is to compare the two formats. We show that the Lorenz curve format tends to produce more efficient but less robust estimators of distributional parameters and of inequality measures. JEL Codes C13, C16, D31
title: Histogram vs Lorenz

abstract: This paper investigates the role of outward multinational enterprise (MNE) networks in shaping regional resilience to financial stress episodes, using regional, sectoral, and firm-level data for the entire sample of NUTS-2 EU regions. The results suggest that regions and sectors with a greater presence of outward-oriented MNE groups—comprising locally headquartered parent firms and their foreign subsidiaries—experience significantly smaller output declines following domestic stress. A Rajan-Zingales-style analysis further shows that sectors characterized by higher external financial dependence are more adversely affected, but this vulnerability is substantially attenuated in regions with larger outward MNE networks. The findings are consistent with the view that MNE networks enhance regional resilience by facilitating access to internal capital markets and cross-border funding when domestic credit conditions deteriorate.
title: Multinational enterprise networks and regional resilience to financial shocks

abstract: Understanding technology adoption processes is crucial for agricultural policy and research, yet most studies rely on mean-based models that may obscure distributional differences. This study investigates precision agriculture technology adoption intensity using survey data collected between December 2024 and January 2025 from 342 German farmers. Adoption intensity is measured as the number of technologies used from a portfolio of 32 technologies and analysed by quantile count regression alongside negative binomial regression. Results reveal that risk attitude shows stable associations with across all quantiles, while farm succession exhibits increasing associations. Results demonstrate limitations of mean-based approaches and provide insights for stakeholders.
title: A quantile count regression analysis of precision agriculture technology adoption intensity

abstract: International climate commitments depend on sustained commitments, yet the United States policy reversals reveal that participation is a recurring political choice rather than a one-time decision. We develop a two-region stochastic integrated assessment model in which US compliance with Paris Agreement aligned emissions caps follows a Markov-switching process, then solve its associated feedback Nash equilibria with state-contingent mitigation and consumption strategies. Our results show that the US climate policy uncertainty generates substantial dispersion in emissions and abatement costs. Moreover, welfare effects are asymmetric: US gains from intermittent free-riding (mean consumption-equivalent variation of $455 per capita per year) while the rest of the world (RoW) incurs losses ($43 per capita per year) driven primarily by higher expected climate damages, with a global aggregate loss of $149 billion per year. Furthermore, when policy uncertainty instead arises in RoW, global effects are muted because their emissions cap remains slack during much of the transition, so spillovers operate mainly through damages rather than strategic mitigation.
journal: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management
source_issue: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management
title: Strategic spillovers of time inconsistency risk in climate commitment

abstract: We propose a cultural transmission model based on the co-evolution of cultural traits, behaviors, and socialization levels. Cultural traits affect agents’ behavior during their interaction in a strategic environment. In turn, behaviors affect how much parents directly socialize their children. The co-evolution of cultural traits and behaviors across two cultural groups microfounds well-established acculturation processes: assimilation, integration, marginalization , and separation . We characterize how the occurrence of each process depends on the nature of the strategic environment (complements or substitutes), on whether material payoffs vary across interactions within a period or remain fixed, and on the costs of transmitting a trait.
title: An Economic Model of Acculturation under Strategic Complements and Substitutes

abstract: What are the macroeconomic and distributional effects of large cash transfers when implemented at scale? We develop a two-region, small open economy heterogeneous-agent model with occupational choice, financial and real frictions, and labor mobility across regions. We discipline the model with baseline data from a new large-scale experiment in rural Malawi. In the model, transfers generate a sharp increase in consumption and a more persistent expansion in productive expenditures, especially intermediate inputs. There is substantial heterogeneity within and across regions: lower-wealth households exhibit the largest consumption response, while wealthier entrepreneurs account for much of the expansion in capital and intermediate input use. Through labor-market spillovers, workers in non-treated regions benefit, whereas entrepreneurs there are adversely affected. These effects gradually dissipate as the economy converges back to its pre-transfer equilibrium.
title: Predicting the effects of a large-scale cash transfer: Financial frictions, occupational choice, and local labor markets

abstract: We examine how disclosure processing costs influence SEC monitoring of firm disclosures by leveraging the mandatory adoption of XBRL—a digital reporting language designed to reduce these costs. Post adoption, both the frequency and quality of SEC comment letters for 10-K filings increase. Additional tests suggest that XBRL enhances SEC monitoring through three channels. First, automated data extraction improves review efficiency, as reflected in more timely comment letters and greater XBRL benefits when the SEC faces tighter resource constraints or uses XBRL analytical tools. Second, standardized reporting strengthens the SEC’s benchmarking ability: firms using more standardized tags and tags more comparable to those of industry peers benefit more. Third, XBRL facilitates SEC scrutiny of complex reporting issues, yielding more frequent and higher-quality comments on noncore earnings accounts and for firms with more footnote tags or complex filings. Overall, our evidence suggests that reduced disclosure processing costs enhance the SEC’s regulatory monitoring.
title: XBRL adoption and SEC monitoring

abstract: This study examines how minimum wage increases affect the mental health of low-wage workers in China. We leverage temporal and county-level variation in minimum wage adjustments from 2010 to 2020 to estimate their causal effects. To identify individuals most likely affected by minimum wage increases, we adopt two complementary strategies: one based on historical wage distributions and another using a demographics-based machine learning approach. We find that minimum wage increases significantly reduce depression among affected workers, whereas no discernible effect is observed for a placebo group of workers less likely to be exposed to the policy. The mental health benefits are especially pronounced among individuals more susceptible to mental illness. Mechanism analyses indicate that these improvements are driven primarily by higher income, increased consumption, and reinforced economic security. By documenting the mental health benefits of minimum wage increases, our research highlights the role of such policies in promoting subjective well-being.

abstract: Physicists could already explain the motion of planets with extraordinary precision centuries ago. Finance still struggles to explain yesterday’s stock market movement. This column identifies a foundational failure of empirical asset pricing and makes significant progress towards explaining market movements using AI. Conventional measures account for remarkably little return variation, even with hindsight. Reasons extracted with AI from just one Wall Street Journal market recap per trading day explain about 30% of daily and 40% of monthly S&P 500 return variation out of sample.
authors: Bryan Kelly, Yinan Su, Chao Zhang
title: Explaining the stock market: Why is it still so hard?

abstract: Advanced economies are counting on artificial intelligence to revive productivity growth just as their workforces age. This column argues that the two trends are closely connected, because young workers adopt new technologies at far higher rates than old workers. Evidence from US local labour markets shows that younger workforces adopt more technology, see faster wage growth, and generate more innovation. A model calibrated to these responses attributes about one quarter of the late-1990s US productivity boom to the baby boom’s youth wave. Workforce ageing is thus a headwind to adoption-driven growth, though it need not diminish the gains from an AI-scale breakthrough.
title: The demographics of technology adoption and productivity growth

abstract: Governments use tax incentives to encourage innovation, but their benefits may extend beyond the firms claiming them. Using the Dutch innovation box and linked employer-employee data, this column shows that firms share part of their additional after-tax profits with incumbent workers, including those not directly engaged in R&D. Higher wages also coincide with lower job-to-job mobility among non-R&D workers. These findings highlight the labour market consequences of innovation policy.
title: Rent sharing under innovation tax breaks

abstract: This study examines the nonlinear relationship between cross-border data flow restrictions and firm resilience using panel data on Chinese A-share manufacturing firms from 2014 to 2022. We find an inverted U-shaped relationship: moderate restrictions enhance resilience by strengthening data security and supply chain efficiency, whereas excessive restrictions weaken resilience by increasing compliance costs and technological rigidity. Digital transformation significantly moderates this relationship by flattening the inverted U-shaped curve. Greater digital transformation attenuates both the resilience-enhancing effect of low-intensity restrictions and the resilience-reducing effect of high-intensity restrictions, reducing firms’ sensitivity to regulatory intensity. Heterogeneity analysis shows that these effects are stronger among firms in eastern regions, technology-intensive firms, and firms with lower supply chain transparency. The findings demonstrate that the resilience effects of cross-border data regulation depend critically on regulatory intensity and firms’ digital capabilities. The results highlight the importance of differentiated policies that balance data security, cross-border data use, and firms’ adaptability within global value chains.

abstract: This paper extends the sustainable-consumption benchmark of Campbell and Martin (2025) to an Epstein–Zin recursive-utility setting. The purpose is not to replace the Campbell–Martin certainty-equivalent mechanism, but to separate two preference channels that are mechanically tied together under time-separable CRRA utility. Risk aversion determines the optimal portfolio and the certainty-equivalent return r CE , and hence the risk-sensitive ceiling in β ⋆ = min { β , r CE } . Conditional on β ⋆ and r CE , the elasticity of intertemporal substitution parameterizes the affine mapping into the sustainable consumption–wealth ratio. Sustainability is formulated as a conditional non-declining requirement on the recursive continuation-welfare process. Thus the criterion is imposed on recursive certainty-equivalent welfare rather than on a time-additive utility sum. Using the conditional non-declining welfare formulation and the sustainable-HJB verification principle for submartingale performance processes, we obtain a closed-form characterization in the Brownian benchmark. The sustainable consumption–wealth ratio is the smaller of the unconstrained Epstein–Zin consumption–wealth ratio and the certainty-equivalent return generated by the Merton portfolio. The risky share remains the Merton share. The contribution is a recursive decomposition into an asset-pricing and discount-rate-ceiling channel, operating through risk aversion, the Merton portfolio, and r CE , and an intertemporal-substitution channel, through which ψ maps ( β ⋆ , r CE ) into the sustainable consumption–wealth ratio.
title: Recursive utility, social discounting, and sustainable consumption
